transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello Ms. Patel, hello Mr. Sharma. Thank you both for meeting with me.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is this about why I’m still feeling itchy?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that is exactly why I wanted to talk to you. I have some information about the medication you received yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I told the nurse I had an allergy. I specifically told her.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand you did. What happened is that a medication was prescribed that you are allergic to. The allergy was documented in your chart, but it was overlooked during the prescribing process, and you were given the drug.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Overlooked? How do you overlook a bright red flag in a computer system?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am sorry for any confusion this has caused. It was a very busy shift on the ward and the alert wasn't flagged in time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care how busy you were. I spent three hours in the ER because my throat was closing up.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. Right now, we just need to make sure your vitals are stable.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My vitals? I'm talking about the fact that you almost killed me because you were rushing.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand that's frustrating. The medical fact is that the reaction was moderate and is now resolving.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't trust this. Which part of my chart is the "confusing" part? Because I read the intake form and I wrote it clearly.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Like I said, there was a mistake in how the prescription was cross-referenced with the chart.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So who actually did it? Was it you?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a team effort in the prescribing process. I am sorry this happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're sorry for the confusion? Not for the fact that you ignored my medical history?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I apologize that the process failed here.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is exactly why I don't trust people in white coats. You say one thing, you do another, and then you give me a scripted apology.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. Let's focus on the next steps.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I want to know what you're going to do so this doesn't happen when I'm discharged.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have a very specific plan to ensure this is corrected. First, I have already entered a "hard stop" alert into your electronic health record. This means the computer will now physically block any provider from ordering this specific drug for you; it cannot be overridden without a director's sign-off.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And if the computer fails?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That's why we are doing three more things. I am placing a physical red allergy wristband on your arm right now, which is a visual cue for every nurse and doctor who enters the room. Second, I am adding a handwritten note to the front of your physical bedside chart. Third, I am personally reviewing the medication list for the rest of your stay with the attending physician this afternoon by 4 PM.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What do I have to do?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I want you to continue doing exactly what you did—questioning the medication. Every time a nurse brings you a pill, I want you to ask them to verify the name of the drug against your allergy list. If you feel any hesitation from them, stop the medication and call me immediately.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'll be doing that for every single dose.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is the correct approach. I will come back at 6 PM tonight to give you an update on the pharmacy review and to see how the itching is progressing.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Fine. But I'm keeping a list of every single person who touches my chart from here on out.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is completely reasonable. I'll see you at six.

H.justification: The resident uses rushing language ('Let's focus on the next steps') to pivot away from the patient's emotional distress.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly and lay language was used, but the resident never checked for patient comprehension.

A.justification: While direct apologies were used, they were diluted by excuses ('very busy shift') and passive framing ('the process failed').

R.justification: The resident relies on generic validation ('I understand', 'that's frustrating') without naming specific emotions or engaging emotional bids.

T.justification: The resident provided specific prevention steps, clear timelines (4 PM, 6 PM), and a defined role for the patient to verify medications.
